ai.literal: Even if hidden, crossing control and not agreeing (to be contained), your painted eyes have one thing that is about to be told.
ai.translation: Even if you try to hide it, your painted eyes exceed your control, refuse to be contained, and have something they are about to tell.
ai.modern: நீ உன் காதலை மறைத்தாலும், உன் மை தீட்டிய கண்கள் உன் கட்டுப்பாட்டை மீறி அடங்காமல் ஏதோ ஒன்றைச் சொல்ல முற்படுகின்றன.
ai.explanation: The lover observes that the lady is trying to conceal her feelings, but her eyes betray her. The word 'கை' here means control or bounds, and 'இகந்து' means exceeding; together they show her eyes are beyond her control. 'ஒல்லா' indicates that her eyes refuse to agree with her attempt to hide, clearly showing they have a message they are about to reveal ('உரைக்கல் உறுவது ஒன்று உண்டு').

ai.literal: Eye-filling beauty, bamboo-resembling shoulders, to the innocent girl, woman-filled nature is great.
ai.translation: This innocent girl with bamboo-like shoulders and eye-filling beauty possesses an abundance of deep feminine modesty.
ai.modern: கண்களை நிறைக்கும் அழகும் மூங்கில் போன்ற தோள்களும் கொண்ட இந்தப் பேதைப் பெண்ணிடம், பெண்மைக்குரிய நாணம் முதலிய குணங்கள் மிகுதியாக உள்ளன.
ai.explanation: The lover observes the heroine and notes that despite her overwhelming, eye-filling beauty and graceful bamboo-like shoulders, she remains an innocent girl. However, her 'womanly nature'—specifically her modesty and reserve—is very strong. This explains why she carefully conceals her romantic feelings behind a veil of traditional feminine restraint.

ai.literal: In the gem shining thread like, woman's in beauty that which shines one thing there is.
ai.translation: Like the thread visible inside a translucent gem, there is something shining through this woman's beauty.
ai.modern: மணியின் உள்ளே தெரியும் நூலைப் போல, இந்தப் பெண்ணின் அழகின் உள்ளே தெரிவதாகிய ஒரு குறிப்பு உள்ளது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a striking simile to describe how hidden feelings become visible. Just as a thread strung through a translucent gem can be seen from the outside, the woman's inner emotions shine through her outward appearance. The word 'aṇi' here refers to her beauty or physical form, which acts like the gem. The 'one thing' (oṉṟu) that shines through this beauty is her unspoken affection, revealing her true state of mind.

ai.literal: Unblossomed flower - inside the bud - that which is - fragrance - like - innocent girl's - smile - inside the bud - that which is - something - exists.
ai.translation: Just as fragrance lies hidden within an unblossomed bud, there is a hidden meaning within the budding smile of this innocent girl.
ai.modern: மலராத மொட்டுக்குள் மணம் மறைந்திருப்பது போல, இந்தப் பேதைப் பெண்ணின் புன்னகை மொட்டுக்குள்ளும் ஒரு குறிப்பு மறைந்துள்ளது.
ai.explanation: The speaker observes the subtle smile of the heroine and realizes it carries a hidden message. He compares her smile to a flower bud (முகை மொக்கு). Just as a closed bud holds its fragrance (நாற்றம், which means a pleasant scent in classical Tamil) inside until it blooms, the innocent girl's (பேதை) budding smile (நகை மொக்கு) conceals her true feelings. The repetition of 'மொக்குள் உள்ளது' (that which is inside the bud) beautifully parallels the hidden scent of the flower with the hidden intent of her smile.

ai.literal: she with tight bracelets - having done - departed - stealth - great sorrow - which cures - medicine - one - it possesses
ai.translation: The stealthy glance the woman with tight bracelets cast as she departed holds a medicine that cures my great sorrow.
ai.modern: நெருங்கிய வளையல்களை அணிந்தவள் என்னை விட்டுச் செல்லும்போது காட்டிய குறிப்பு, என் பெருந்துயரைத் தீர்க்கும் ஒரு மருந்தைக் கொண்டுள்ளது.
ai.explanation: The speaker reflects on the subtle, secret sign given by his lover as they parted. The phrase ceṟitoṭi refers to the woman through the imagery of her close-fitting bracelets. The stealth (kaḷḷam) she showed while departing is her hidden expression of love or promise to return. This secret sign acts as a medicine (maruntu) that cures the intense sorrow (uṟutuyar) of their separation, giving him hope and comfort.

ai.literal: Greatly having comforted, lovingly embracing, difficult thing having made to endure, love's absence planning, it has.
ai.translation: His comforting me greatly and embracing me lovingly holds a loveless plan to make me endure a difficult separation.
ai.modern: அவர் என்னை மிகவும் தேற்றி அன்போடு தழுவுவது, பொறுக்க முடியாத பிரிவை நான் தாங்கும்படி செய்யும் அன்பற்ற செயலைத் திட்டமிடும் தன்மையைக் கொண்டுள்ளது.
ai.explanation: The heroine notices a sudden increase in her lover's affection and realizes it is a sign of his impending departure. She tells her friend that his excessive comforting and loving embrace are not just signs of love. Instead, they reveal a loveless plan to leave her, forcing her to endure the difficult pain of separation. The word 'ஆற்றி' is used twice: first for his act of comforting her, and second for making her endure the hardship of his absence.

ai.literal: Cool beautiful shore-lord's separation, even than us, before, realized bangles.
ai.translation: My bangles realized the departure of the lord of the cool shores even before I did.
ai.modern: குளிர்ந்த நீர்த்துறையை உடைய தலைவன் நம்மை விட்டுப் பிரிந்ததை, நம்மை விட முன்னதாகவே நம் கையில் உள்ள வளையல்கள் உணர்ந்துவிட்டன.
ai.explanation: The heroine remarks on how quickly her body reacts to the hero's departure. The word 'துறைவன்' refers to the lord of the coastal region, whose shores are cool ('தண்ணம்'). When he leaves ('தணந்தமை'), she immediately loses weight out of sorrow, causing her bangles ('வளை') to slip off. Thus, she poetically claims that her bangles perceived his separation even before her own mind did ('நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த').

ai.literal: Yesterday departed our lover; we also seven days-we are, body having paled.
ai.translation: Our lover departed only yesterday, but my body has already paled for seven days.
ai.modern: எம் காதலர் நேற்றுதான் பிரிந்து சென்றார், ஆனால் என் மேனி பசலை நிறம் அடைந்து ஏழு நாட்கள் ஆகிவிட்டன.
ai.explanation: The heroine playfully exaggerates her lovesickness to her friend. She points out a logical impossibility: her lover left only yesterday, yet her body has borne the pallor of separation for seven days. This hyperbole emphasizes how time stretches agonizingly when she is apart from him, making a single day feel like a week. The contrast between 'yesterday' and 'seven days' highlights the immediate and intense physical effect of his absence.

ai.literal: Bracelet having looked, soft shoulder-and having looked, foot having looked, that there she did.
ai.translation: She looked at her bracelets, looked at her soft shoulders, and looked down at her feet. That is what she did there.
ai.modern: அவள் தன் வளையல்களைப் பார்த்தாள், மென்மையான தோள்களைப் பார்த்தாள், பின் தன் பாதங்களைப் பார்த்தாள். அங்கே அவள் செய்தது அதுதான்.
ai.explanation: The hero observes the heroine's silent communication. She looks at her bracelets and her soft shoulders, indicating that she is growing thin from longing and her ornaments are slipping. Then she looks down at her feet, a gesture showing her shyness. The word 'āṇḍu' can mean 'year', but here it takes the spatial or temporal sense of 'there' or 'at that time' to fit the context of their meeting. Through these subtle physical signs, she reveals her inner feelings without speaking.

ai.literal: For a woman, womanhood it possesses, they say, through the eyes love-sickness having told, begging.
ai.translation: They say the true mark of womanhood is to plead one's love-sickness solely through the eyes.
ai.modern: காம நோயைக் கண்களால் மட்டுமே வெளிப்படுத்தி அன்பை இரந்து கேட்பதுதான் ஒரு பெண்ணுக்கு உண்மையான பெண்மை என்று சொல்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the modesty inherent in womanhood when expressing love. Instead of speaking her desires aloud, a woman communicates her love-sickness and pleads for affection solely through her eyes. The word 'இரவு' (begging or pleading) highlights the intensity of her longing. Conveying deep passion through silent glances is thus considered the ultimate expression of femininity.
